name: Cryptographic Hash
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: When a Fingerprint Has to Be Tamper-Proof
lesson.summary: A cryptographic hash function is a hash function with strong security guarantees, preimage resistance, second preimage resistance, and collision resistance, that make it safe to use against an adversary rather than just against random chance.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter described a hash function as anything that squeezes arbitrary input into a fixed-size output, quickly and deterministically. That definition is enough for organizing a hash table, but it says nothing about what happens when someone is actively trying to break the system. A cryptographic hash function is a hash function that adds a much stronger set of guarantees on top of the ordinary ones, guarantees designed to hold up even against an adversary who is deliberately searching for weaknesses rather than stumbling into them by accident.

Three properties define a secure cryptographic hash function. Preimage resistance means that given a hash output, it should be computationally infeasible to find any input that produces it. In other words, you cannot work backward from the fingerprint to the original document. Second preimage resistance means that given one specific input, it should be infeasible to find a different input that produces the exact same hash as that first one. Collision resistance is the broadest of the three: it should be infeasible to find any two different inputs, chosen freely rather than starting from a fixed one, that happen to produce the same hash. These are subtly different guarantees, and a function can in principle satisfy one while failing another, which is why cryptographers define all three separately rather than treating "hard to fool" as one blanket property.

Collision resistance in particular has a mathematical wrinkle worth understanding, known as the birthday bound. Because a hash function maps an effectively infinite space of possible inputs down to a finite number of possible outputs, collisions must exist somewhere; the guarantee is only that they are astronomically hard to find on purpose. For an output that is n bits long, brute-force collision search takes roughly two to the power of n divided by two attempts, not two to the power of n, because you are just looking for any two matching outputs among many random tries, not matching a specific target. This is why cryptographic hash functions use output sizes, commonly 256 bits, that are far larger than what preimage resistance alone would require, to keep the birthday-bound math on the defender's side.

The practical consequence of these properties is that a cryptographic hash becomes trustworthy as tamper-evidence, not merely as a data-organizing shortcut. If a cryptographic hash of a file matches a previously published value, you can be confident, based on real mathematical hardness assumptions rather than convenience, that the file has not been altered and that no one could have engineered a different file to match the same hash. This is the property that later chapters build on directly: it is what lets a block in a blockchain reference the previous block's hash and have that reference actually mean something, and it is what lets a signature over a hash of a message stand in securely for a signature over the whole message itself. The next chapter looks at SHA-256, the specific cryptographic hash function that underlies most of what modern blockchains do.
